title: Number parsing, validation and range expansion
summary: E.164 normalization and turning rules into exact number lists for iOS
description:
CURRENT STATE: nothing built in Rust. The arithmetic is proven by throwaway Python prototypes in the session scratchpad (expand.py, generic.py) which ran against real libphonenumber metadata across all 245 territories; those are reference only.

NORMALIZATION: normalize(raw, defaultRegion) -> E164. Use the `phonenumber` crate (0.3.10+9.0.33) for parse/validate/format.

EXPANSION — the part iOS calls depend on: expand(Rule, limit) -> sorted exact numbers, or TooBroad(count). Driven by possibleLengths AND nationalNumberPattern, per country per number type, from F003's datasets.

THE REGEX MUST PRUNE. Summing possible lengths alone materially overestimates. Worst case measured: DE fixedLine has ELEVEN possible lengths (5 to 15), so a naive sum gives 11,111,111,111,000 for "+49 30" where the validating pattern rejects most of it. The prototype only summed lengths and is knowingly wrong here — the real implementation must apply the pattern.

ALLOW-EXCEPTIONS BY SUBTRACTION: CallKit has no allow list, so an allow rule inside a deny is resolved here by simply not emitting that number — 999 entries instead of 1000. No runtime support needed on iOS.

OUTPUT ORDER: iOS requires strictly ascending int64 with no duplicates (addBlockingEntry(withNextSequentialPhoneNumber:)). Generate in order and assert monotonicity — an out-of-order entry fails the whole extension request.

STREAMING, NOT MATERIALISING: the iOS extension runs under tight memory limits, so expansion must yield incrementally rather than build a full Vec.

THE LIMIT IS INJECTED: the maximum entry count comes from F001's measurement as configuration, never a constant (Guidelines §4). explain(Rule) returns the expansion count and per-platform verdict for R2's honesty requirement.

MEASURED CONTEXT: 226/244 countries need <=4 digits pinned for mobile, 223/245 for landline. Hard tail: DE fixedLine 10 digits, AT mobile 8, DE mobile 6, IT fixedLine 7.

tasks.title: Normalize raw input to E.164
tasks.description:
CURRENT STATE. core/src/evaluate.rs defines E164<'a>, which borrows and validates shape only — it refuses anything that is not digits with an optional leading `+`. Nothing produces one from what a user or an OS actually hands over. The phonenumber crate (0.3.10+9.0.33) is already a dependency (core/Cargo.toml) and is currently unused.

GOAL. normalize(raw: &str, default_region) -> Result<Normalized, ParseError>, in core/src/normalize.rs (new). Two callers, and they differ:
- The OS hands over a number when a call or message arrives. Android gives a tel: URI from Call.Details; iOS SMS gives ILMessageFilterQueryRequest.sender.
- The user types a number when writing a rule, often in national form with no country code.

VERIFIED API, checked against the crate source on 2026-09-09:
- phonenumber::parse(Option<Country>, raw) -> Result<PhoneNumber, ParseError>
- phonenumber::metadata::DATABASE is the bundled database; Database::by_id(region) -> Option<&Metadata>
- PhoneNumber formats to E.164 via phonenumber::format(&n).mode(Mode::E164)
Do not re-derive this; do confirm the exact signatures compile rather than trusting this note.

WHAT TO BUILD:
1. normalize() producing an owned normalized number that E164::new accepts. E164 borrows, so return an owning type and let callers borrow from it — do not fight the lifetime by allocating inside evaluate.
2. A default region for the "user typed a national number" case. It is a parameter, never a constant: Guidelines §1 forbids a country in code. The shells pass the device region.
3. Distinguish, in the error, between input that is not a number at all and input that parses but is not valid for its region. The UI must say something different for each — "that is not a number" versus "that is not a valid number in this country" — and R2's honesty rule means never quietly accepting the second.

CONSTRAINTS.
- Guidelines §1: no country, prefix or length in code. The default region is data passed in.
- Guidelines §4: nothing measured written as a literal.
- Runs on the Android call path inside the five-second screening budget, so parsing must not be gratuitously slow, though this is far cheaper than the budget.

EDGE CASES to test: a number already in E.164; a national number with the default region supplied; a national number with no region supplied (must fail, not guess); leading/trailing whitespace and the separators users type; an extension; a short code; a number valid in one region and not another; empty input; letters.

DONE WHEN. normalize() feeds evaluate() end to end in a test, both error cases are distinguishable, and cargo test / fmt / clippy -D warnings / tools/check-no-hardcoded-numbering.sh pass. Number-shaped fixtures go in core/tests/, not core/src — the §1 lint scans core/src and that strictness is worth keeping.

**Completion summary:**
SHIPPED. Commit e0b122e.

core/src/normalize.rs (new) and core/tests/normalize.rs (new, 11 tests). core/src/lib.rs re-exports normalize, Normalized, NormalizeError. The phonenumber crate was a declared dependency and unused until now; this is its first use.

API. normalize(raw: &str, default_region: Option<&str>, database: &Database) -> Result<Normalized, NormalizeError>. Normalized owns its E.164 text; Normalized::number() borrows it as E164, so the call path allocates nothing to evaluate. Invariant: the stored string always starts with '+'.

BUG FOUND AND FIXED — the important part of this task. Passing the device region alongside a number that already carries its own country code corrupts it. phonenumber::parse_with applies the hint region's national-prefix rule even to an international number, and countries disagree about the trunk digit. Probed directly against the crate:
  +390212345678 with no hint  -> national 0212345678, valid
  +390212345678 with hint DE  -> national 212345678,  INVALID
  +390212345678 with hint IT  -> national 0212345678, valid
Italy keeps a leading 0 in the national number; Germany strips one. So a user in Germany writing a rule for an Italian number would have been told the number does not exist. The fix withholds the region whenever the input already starts with '+', which is also the semantically right rule: the region is for reading a national number, and that is not one. Regression test covers both directions (IT number with DE hint, DE number with IT hint). This was found by probing the crate rather than by reasoning — the first version of the code documented the correct behaviour in a comment and did not implement it.

VERIFIED API, probed against phonenumber 0.3.10+9.0.33 rather than assumed: parse_with(&Database, Option<country::Id>, S); is_valid_with(&Database, &PhoneNumber); format(&n).mode(Mode::E164); country::Id derives FromStr via strum EnumString, so a region arrives as a plain string from the shell.

DECISION — the database is a parameter, not the crate's bundled global. R5 requires metadata updates without an app release, and Database::load / Database::parse exist, so F003's over-the-air dataset can replace it. Reaching for DATABASE inside would have closed that off. Callers must supply one; no convenience wrapper using the global was added, deliberately.

DECISION — four distinct errors, because the user needs a different sentence for each and R2 forbids quietly accepting something that can never match. NotANumber; RegionRequired (national input with no region — refused rather than guessed, since guessing silently builds a rule against another country's numbers); UnknownRegion (the shell supplied a region the data does not know, which signals a misconfigured shell); NotValidForRegion (parses but no such number exists). No user-facing wording is in the core — R7 makes UI text a data file.

VERIFIED. cargo test: 61 pass (15 unit, 11 normalize, 17 evaluate, 18 rule_model), 0 fail. cargo fmt --check clean. cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings clean. tools/check-no-hardcoded-numbering.sh passes. UniFFI binding generation re-run and still succeeds. End-to-end test proves a rule typed nationally matches a call delivered internationally, which is the reason normalization exists.

TEST FIXTURE CORRECTED. A first test used +3900000 expecting NotValidForRegion; that input fails at parse with MalformedInteger, so it never reached validation. Replaced with +3902123, which parses and is invalid — confirmed by probe.

UNVERIFIED. Nothing has run on a device or been called from Swift or Kotlin. The five-second Android budget is not measured against; parsing is far cheaper than that, but this is reasoning, not measurement. Only IT, DE and US were probed — the trunk-digit fix is general, but no systematic sweep across all 245 territories was done. P003(F002)/T012 will exercise every territory and is the natural place for that to surface.

NOT DONE HERE. No expansion (T010), no explain (T011). A tel: URI is not unwrapped — the Android shell passes the number part; if that turns out to be wrong it belongs in the shell, not here.

tasks.title: Range expansion for iOS, regex-pruned and streaming
tasks.description:
DEPENDS ON P003(F002)/T006 for normalization, and on the rule model in P002(F002)/T004.

WHY THIS EXISTS. iOS runs no app code when a call arrives, so rules cannot be evaluated live there. They are turned into a list of exact numbers ahead of time and handed to CallKit. This is the only shipped surface where a rule cannot run live, and it is where R2's promise meets a hard platform limit.

GOAL. expand(rule, metadata, limit) yielding ascending int64 numbers, or reporting TooBroad(count), in core/src/expand.rs (new).

THE REGEX MUST PRUNE — this is the whole point of the task. Summing possibleLengths alone materially overestimates. Measured worst case: DE fixedLine has ELEVEN possible lengths (5 to 15), so a naive sum gives 11,111,111,111,000 entries for a two-digit prefix, where the validating pattern rejects the overwhelming majority. The Python prototypes that produced the plan's figures only summed lengths and are knowingly wrong here. Do not reproduce that.

VERIFIED API, checked against the crate source on 2026-09-09 — confirm it compiles, do not trust this note blindly:
- phonenumber::metadata::DATABASE, and Database::by_id(region) -> Option<&Metadata>
- Metadata::descriptors() -> &Descriptors; Descriptors::get(Type) -> Option<&Descriptor>
- Descriptor::possible_length() -> &[u16]
- Descriptor::is_match(&str) -> bool, which applies nationalNumberPattern
Descriptors::get returns Option because not every country defines every type — do not assume a fixed set (Guidelines §1).
Database::load(path) and Database::parse(content) exist, so F003's over-the-air dataset can replace the bundled one later. Take the database as a parameter rather than reaching for DATABASE inside, or that future is closed off.

EXPANDABILITY DIFFERS BY MATCHER, and this must be explicit rather than discovered:
- Exact: one number.
- StartsWith / Prefix: the range under that prefix, pruned by the validating pattern per possible length.
- Pattern: the cartesian product over wildcard positions, pruned the same way.
- EndsWith: enumerating every valid number with a given tail means walking a country's whole number space. This will almost always be too broad for iOS. Report it honestly rather than attempting it and timing out.
- CallerId: cannot be expanded at all. iOS calls have no caller-ID matching, so such a rule simply does not apply there and the user must be told.

ALLOW-EXCEPTIONS BY SUBTRACTION. CallKit has no allow list, so an allow rule inside a deny is resolved here by not emitting those numbers — 999 entries instead of 1000. An allow rule with no enclosing deny expands to nothing, because absence already means allowed.

OUTPUT CONTRACT. Strictly ascending int64, no duplicates. iOS requires this (addBlockingEntry withNextSequentialPhoneNumber:) and an out-of-order entry fails the entire extension request, not just that entry. Generate in order and assert monotonicity in a test rather than sorting afterwards.

STREAMING, NOT MATERIALISING. The extension runs under tight memory limits. Yield incrementally; never build a full Vec of a million numbers. An Iterator is the obvious shape.

THE LIMIT IS INJECTED. The maximum entry count comes from F001's measurement as configuration (EntryLimit in core/src/lib.rs), never a constant (Guidelines §4). Counting must stop early once the limit is exceeded — do not count to eleven trillion to report TooBroad.

EDGE CASES to test: a prefix that expands to exactly the limit, and one over it; a pattern where the validating regex rejects most candidates; a rule for a country whose descriptor for that type is absent; an allow fully inside a deny; an allow only partly overlapping a deny; two denies that overlap, so a number would otherwise be emitted twice; an EndsWith rule; a CallerId rule.

DONE WHEN. Expansion is correct and ascending, the regex demonstrably prunes (a test asserting a count far below the naive length-sum for a real multi-length country), counting stops early past the limit, memory stays flat for a large expansion, and cargo test / fmt / clippy -D warnings / tools/check-no-hardcoded-numbering.sh pass. Fixtures in core/tests/.

---
**Completion summary:**
SHIPPED. Commit cfe4f0c. Two checklist items left deliberately open — see below.

core/src/expand.rs (new) and core/tests/expand.rs (new, 16 tests). core/src/rule.rs gained Pattern::slots() and Pattern::fixed_prefix(). lib.rs re-exports expand_matcher, expand_rules, Budget, Expansion, NotExpandable.

THE TASK'S PREMISE WAS WRONG, and this is the main finding. The task (and R2, and the phase) say the validating pattern must be applied because summing possibleLengths "materially overestimates, badly for landlines", citing DE fixedLine at 11 trillion. Probed against the bundled metadata on 2026-09-10:
- The pattern constrains LEADING digits, not the tail. 72 of 100 two-digit DE fixed-line prefixes are accepted; the rest (00, 11, ...) are rejected outright.
- Once a prefix is accepted, EVERY completion at EVERY possible length is accepted. Sampled 20,000 tails for DE prefix 30 and IT prefix 02 at every possible length: density 1.000 throughout.
- So for Germany and Italy the pattern prunes NOTHING, and the Python prototype's 11 trillion was CORRECT, not an artifact of summing lengths.
- Swept all 245 territories: 165 have a viable two-digit fixed-line prefix, and 37 of those show a tail density below 1. Worst observed LI at 0.095 — roughly tenfold. Never orders of magnitude.

CONSEQUENCES, which shaped the design.
1. Applying the pattern is still necessary, but for a different reason than the plan gives: it keeps numbers that do not exist out of the list. An unused Italian area code now expands to nothing instead of thousands of fictional entries. There is a test for exactly that.
2. It can never rescue a rule from being too broad. A tenfold cut to 10^13 is 10^12.
3. Therefore expansion SIZE is arithmetic, not enumeration. The ceiling is the sum over possible lengths of 10^(L-p), computed with saturating arithmetic. The German case is answered in microseconds. A test asserts it completes in under five seconds and would fail if this regressed to enumeration.
4. Item C4 on the checklist — "test asserting the pruned count is far below the naive length-sum" — is left OPEN because it asks for something that is not true. No such test can pass for DE or IT. The test that replaced it asserts the pattern excludes non-existent numbers instead.

DESIGN. One generator, not one per matcher. A Template is the national number position by position, each slot fixed or varying. A prefix becomes one template per possible length (union across all of the country's type descriptors, deduped, so two types sharing a length do not double count); a pattern becomes one; an exact number becomes one with nothing varying. An odometer over the varying positions walks them ascending, which is already numerically ascending because every number in one expansion shares a prefix and a longer number is always the larger. Monotonicity is asserted in tests, never fixed by sorting.

DECISION — precedence is not decided twice. expand_rules puts every candidate through evaluate(), so a number on the iOS list is exactly one Android would block live. Allow-exceptions fall out of that rather than needing their own subtraction logic, and there is a test asserting the two surfaces agree number for number.

Suffix and caller-ID rules are reported NotExpandable rather than attempted. Both evaluate live on Android; neither can become a list. Also reported: digits belonging to no country code, and a pattern whose leading digits vary so it belongs to no country.

Number types come from libphonenumber's fixed taxonomy via the named getters, each Optional because a territory defines only some. Short codes and emergency numbers are excluded deliberately — not dialable E.164, cannot appear as a caller.

VERIFIED. cargo test: 93 pass (18 unit, 16 expand, 17 evaluate, 11 normalize, 18 rule_model, 13 others), 0 fail. cargo fmt --check clean. cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings clean. tools/check-no-hardcoded-numbering.sh passes. UniFFI bindings still generate.

NOT DONE — C10, memory. expand_matcher streams and holds nothing. expand_rules does NOT: it collects into a Vec to sort and dedup, which at 1.8M entries is about 14MB inside an extension chosen for its tight memory limit. The fix is a k-way merge over the per-rule iterators, which are each already ascending, so no buffer is needed. Not attempted here. No memory measurement was taken either way, so C10 is left open rather than claimed. This must be resolved before the iOS extension in F004 uses it.

UNVERIFIED. Nothing has run on a device or through Swift or Kotlin. Throughput measured on host only: Descriptor::is_match costs about 2.3µs per candidate with a reused buffer, so a full 1.8M expansion is a few seconds of background work. That is consistent with the 12s CallKit load measured in F001 but has not been observed together on hardware. The 10x candidate allowance in Budget comes from the worst density observed across the bundled metadata; a future metadata update could be worse.

FOLLOW-ON. R2's description still carries the wrong premise ("the expander must apply the validating regex, not merely sum possible lengths — summing materially overestimates") and its pessimistic digit figures. P003(F002)/T012 was written to recompute those figures; it now also needs to correct the premise. The figures will move less than expected, because the prototype was not wrong in the way the plan assumed.

tasks.title: explain(rule): expansion size and per-platform verdict
tasks.description:
DEPENDS ON P003(F002)/T010 for the expansion count.

WHY THIS EXISTS. R2's honesty requirement: show each rule's computed expansion size and per-platform verdict from real data, and never silently drop, narrow or partially apply a rule. This is the function that makes that possible, and it is what R8's UI reads. Without it the app either lies by omission or the user discovers a rule does nothing when a call gets through.

GOAL. explain(rule, database, limits) -> Explanation, in core/src/explain.rs (new).

THE VERDICTS DIFFER BY PLATFORM, and each is a fact already verified in F001 — read F001's description for the evidence rather than re-deriving:
- Android calls: every rule type evaluates live. No expansion, no limit, always applies. The exception is a withheld caller, which never reaches a screening service at all — no rule can ever act on one, and users will expect otherwise.
- iOS SMS: every rule type evaluates live. Verdict caps at the Junk folder, not deletion, and only for unknown senders.
- iOS calls: pre-expanded only. A rule fits, or it is too broad, or it cannot be expressed at all. A CallerId rule cannot apply. An EndsWith rule will almost always be too broad. An allow rule with no enclosing deny is a no-op, and the UI must not imply otherwise.
- Android SMS: out of scope entirely (R2, decided 2026-09-08) — blocking there means becoming the default SMS app.

WHAT TO BUILD. An Explanation carrying, per rule: the expansion count where one applies, and a per-surface verdict that distinguishes at least: applies live; fits within the budget; too broad for this platform; cannot be expressed on this platform; and no effect. Those are distinct user-facing situations and collapsing them loses the honesty R2 asks for.

CONSTRAINTS.
- Guidelines §1: no country, prefix or length in code; no platform's limit written as a literal.
- Guidelines §4: the entry budget is injected configuration from F001's measurement, never a constant.
- Guidelines §5 and R8: the user sees plain language, never an entry count presented as a setting. This function returns facts; wording is the shell's job. Do not put user-facing English in the core — R7 makes UI text a data file, not code.
- The surfaces themselves must be data-driven enough that adding one (HarmonyOS is explicitly contemplated in F002) does not mean rewriting this.

EDGE CASES to test: a rule that fits on iOS and applies live on Android; one too broad for iOS but fine on Android; a CallerId rule, which is live on Android and inexpressible on iOS calls; an allow with no enclosing deny; a rule whose country descriptor for that type is absent; a rule whose expansion is exactly at the limit.

DONE WHEN. Every verdict above is produced from real metadata, no user-facing wording lives in the core, the budget is injected, and cargo test / fmt / clippy -D warnings / tools/check-no-hardcoded-numbering.sh pass. Fixtures in core/tests/.

---
**Completion summary:**
SHIPPED. Commit e05dd08.

core/src/explain.rs (new) and core/tests/explain.rs (new, 11 tests). lib.rs re-exports explain, Explanation, Surface, and Verdict as PlatformVerdict (renamed at the boundary because evaluate::Verdict already exists and means something else — one is what happened to a call, the other what a rule will do).

API. explain(rule, rules, database, surfaces) -> Explanation { rule, verdicts: Vec<(String, Verdict)> }, with Explanation::on(surface_id) to read one.

DECISION — a surface is data, not a match arm. Surface { id, evaluates_live, matches_caller_id, budget }. These are five different things to tell the person who wrote the rule, and collapsing any two loses exactly what R2 asks for. No English anywhere in them; wording is the shell's, per R7.

The rule set is a parameter because an allow's effect depends on what encloses it. changes_anything() reuses Matcher::can_overlap from T004 rather than reimplementing overlap.

TWO CASES THAT WOULD OTHERWISE BE INVISIBLE.
1. A caller-ID rule applies live on Android and on iOS messages, and cannot apply to iOS calls at all — there is no name there. Not too big, not broken: inexpressible, which is a different sentence.
2. A rule for numbers that do not exist expands cleanly to zero entries. The rule is valid, will never fire, and nothing else in the system would ever say so. Reported as NoEffect on a listed surface, while a live surface honestly still says AppliesLive, because it cannot know in advance that nothing will match.

VERIFIED. cargo test: 98 pass, 0 fail. cargo fmt --check clean. cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings clean. tools/check-no-hardcoded-numbering.sh passes. UniFFI bindings still generate. Includes a test that a rule exactly the size of the budget fits, because an off-by-one there means telling someone their rule is too big when it is not.

UNVERIFIED. Nothing has run on a device or through Swift or Kotlin. The surface descriptions in the tests are fixtures written from F001's findings; no shell constructs one yet, so whether this shape is convenient for the UI is unproven until F004 and F005.

NOT DONE HERE. Nothing is exported over UniFFI — the FFI surface is P005(F002). The Android-SMS surface is deliberately absent: R2 put it out of scope on 2026-09-08.

tasks.title: Recompute R2's digit distribution against the measured cap
tasks.description:
DEPENDS ON P003(F002)/T010 — this uses the real expander.

WHY THIS EXISTS. R2 currently states: 226/244 countries need 4 digits or fewer pinned for mobile, 223/245 for landline, with a hard tail of DE fixedLine 10, AT mobile 8, DE mobile 6, IT fixedLine 7. Both halves of that are wrong, in opposite directions, and the numbers are quoted in the requirement as if measured:

1. They were computed against an assumed cap of 1,000,000. The cap was measured on 2026-09-08 as between 1,900,000 and 2,000,000 (P001(F001)/T001). Roughly double the budget means fewer digits need pinning, so the published figures are PESSIMISTIC — the product promises less than it can deliver.

2. They came from Python prototypes that only SUMMED possibleLengths and never applied the validating pattern. That overestimates expansion badly, which pushes the figures pessimistic again, and much harder for landlines. DE fixedLine summed to 11 trillion, which is not a real number of German landlines.

So the figures are wrong twice over, both times in the direction of understating what the app can do. Fixing them changes what the UI can promise and is easy to forget, because nothing fails while they are wrong.

GOAL. Recompute the distribution across every territory in the database, using T010's expander with the validating pattern applied and the measured cap injected. Produce, per country and number type, the smallest number of pinned digits whose expansion fits the budget.

WHAT TO PRODUCE:
1. A test or example in core/ that computes this from the current metadata and is runnable on demand. Not a fixture pasted into a file — metadata changes, and R5 makes over-the-air updates a requirement, so a figure that cannot be recomputed will rot exactly like the current one has.
2. The recomputed summary written into R2's description via the planner, replacing the stale figures, with a note saying which cap and which method produced them.
3. The new hard tail — the countries and types that still need the most digits pinned. These are the cases the UI has to be honest about, so they matter more than the headline count.

CONSTRAINTS.
- Guidelines §1: no country in code. Enumerate territories from the database (Database::iter exists), never from a list in a source file.
- Guidelines §4: the cap is injected configuration from F001, never a literal. Report which value produced the figures.
- This is analysis over 245 territories and many lengths, so it may be slow. Do not put it in the default test run if it takes long enough to hurt CI — mark it ignored and say in the completion note how to run it.

HONESTY. Report what is computed, including any territory the expander cannot handle, rather than quietly excluding it from the denominator. The current figures say 244 and 245 for two different types without explaining the difference; the new ones should account for every territory or say why not.

DONE WHEN. The figures are recomputed from real metadata with the regex applied and the measured cap, R2's description is updated through the planner and read back to confirm it persisted, and the recomputation is repeatable by a documented command.

---
**Completion summary:**
SHIPPED. Commit a8b51d5. R2's description updated through the planner and read back — stale figures gone, new ones present, wrong premise corrected, recompute command included. One checklist item left open on purpose, below.

core/tests/distribution.rs (new): an ignored analysis that walks every territory and prints a report, plus one always-on test. core/src/expand.rs split into prepare/finish, with a new public upper_bound(matcher, database) that returns the ceiling without generating anything. core/tests/expand_memory.rs rewritten (see the CI note below).

THE HEADLINE, and it is the opposite of what the task predicted. The task said the old figures were pessimistic and would improve. They got WORSE:
  old (quoted in R2): 226/244 mobile, 223/245 landline need <=4 digits
  new:                193/242 mobile, 194/242 landline, of 246 territories

The reason is METHOD, not data. The old figures counted one number type in isolation. This counts every number under a prefix regardless of type, because that is what actually goes on the block list — a phone does not skip a number for being a mobile rather than a landline. The old figures described something the product never does. Both numbers are "correct" for what they measured; only one of them is about this product.

NEW HARD TAIL: DE mobile 9 digits; KR, KZ, NG, RU 8; AT, IN, PH, TH, TR 7. Never fits at any prefix length: DE landline, JP and ID both kinds. Not enough metadata: territory 001, and TA for mobile. All 246 territories are accounted for in one of those buckets — the old figures gave 244 and 245 for two types without explaining the difference, and that gap is now closed.

TWO BELIEFS CORRECTED IN R2:
1. The cap doubling from an assumed 1,000,000 to the measured ~1,900,000 buys well under one extra digit, so it helps far less than the task assumed.
2. R2 said "the expander must apply the validating regex, not merely sum possible lengths — summing materially overestimates, badly for landlines". That is wrong, measured in T010 and now recorded in R2. The pattern constrains leading digits, not the tail. What it is actually for is keeping numbers that do not exist off the list.

CHECKLIST ITEM LEFT OPEN — C2, "validating pattern applied, not possibleLengths summed". The count here IS the sum over possible lengths, deliberately. T010 established that for a viable prefix the pattern does not reduce it, except in 37 of 165 territories and by at most about tenfold. The pattern is applied where it matters: prefixes are taken from each descriptor's own example number, so every prefix measured is one the pattern accepts rather than a shape invented here. Ticking C2 would claim a method the measurements say is pointless. Where the tail does constrain, this reports one digit more than strictly needed — conservative in the safe direction.

GUARD ADDED. the_ceiling_is_never_below_what_is_actually_generated runs in the normal suite and asserts upper_bound never promises fewer numbers than the expander delivers. Every figure above rests on that ceiling, and an optimistic one would be wrong in the dangerous direction: telling a user a rule fits when the phone will reject it.

REPEATABLE, not pasted. The analysis prints rather than asserting a fixture, because metadata changes and R5 makes over-the-air updates a requirement — a pasted number rots exactly the way R2's did. Run it with:
  cargo test --release --test distribution -- --ignored --nocapture

CI FIX FOUND ALONG THE WAY. The T013 memory tests took 73 seconds in a debug build, which is what CI runs, so every push paid it. They now compare the streaming and collecting paths against each other on a smaller expansion, in under two seconds. That comparison first reported streaming as WORSE than collecting: whichever path is measured first pays for the metadata regex caches, which populate lazily. The caches are warmed before measuring now. The absolute byte threshold it replaced only ever passed because a million numbers dwarfed that fixed overhead.

VERIFIED. cargo test: 98 pass, 1 ignored, 0 fail. cargo fmt --check clean. cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings clean. tools/check-no-hardcoded-numbering.sh passes. No country appears in code — territories come from Database::iter, prefixes from each descriptor's example.

UNVERIFIED. The cap of 1,800,000 is the default from one device; the real cap is between 1.9M and 2.0M and may differ elsewhere, so every figure moves if that changes — which is the point of it being injected. Nothing here has run on a device.

tasks.title: Stream rule-set expansion instead of collecting it
tasks.description:
FOLLOWS P003(F002)/T010, which left this open rather than claiming it done.

THE PROBLEM. core/src/expand.rs::expand_rules returns Vec<i64>. It collects every number, then sorts and dedups. At the measured iOS budget of 1.8M entries that is roughly 14MB held at once, inside the Call Directory extension — which is exactly the process chosen for its tight memory limit. expand_matcher already streams and holds nothing; the rule-set layer above it undoes that.

Nobody notices until the extension is killed on a real phone with a large rule set, and F001 already established that iOS tells the app nothing when it fails at call time. So this is a silent failure waiting for the worst moment.

WHY IT CAN BE FIXED CHEAPLY. Each rule's expansion is already produced in ascending order — that is guaranteed and tested in T010. So the merged stream needs no buffer: a k-way merge over the per-rule iterators yields ascending output directly, where k is the number of deny rules, which is small. Deduplication is just "skip a value equal to the one just emitted", because the merge is ordered.

WHAT TO BUILD.
1. Replace the Vec with an iterator that merges the per-rule Numbers streams. A BinaryHeap of (value, stream index) with reversed ordering is the obvious shape; k is tiny so the heap costs nothing.
2. Keep the existing behaviour exactly: ascending, no duplicates, and every candidate still passes through evaluate() so the iOS list agrees with what Android decides live. Do not reimplement precedence.
3. Keep a convenience that collects to a Vec if callers want one, but it must not be what the extension path uses.

PROVE IT, do not assert it. T010 claimed nothing about memory because nothing was measured. Install a counting global allocator in an integration test — an integration test compiles to its own binary, so #[global_allocator] is available there — and assert peak live bytes stay bounded while streaming an expansion far larger than the buffer would have been. A test that only checks the output is unchanged does not close this item.

CONSTRAINTS.
- Guidelines §1: no country, prefix or length in code.
- Guidelines §4: the budget stays injected configuration.
- The output contract is unchanged and is not negotiable: strictly ascending int64, no duplicates. iOS fails the entire request otherwise, not just the offending entry.

EDGE CASES to test: no deny rules; one deny rule; several denies that overlap heavily; a deny whose expansion is empty because the pattern rejects it; an allow carving a number out of the middle of a merged run; streams of very different lengths, so one is exhausted long before the others.

DONE WHEN. expand_rules streams, peak memory is measured and bounded by a test rather than argued, every T010 expansion test still passes unchanged, and cargo test / fmt / clippy -D warnings / tools/check-no-hardcoded-numbering.sh pass.

---
**Completion summary:**
SHIPPED. Commits 1d88f59 and f563f01.

core/src/expand.rs: expand_rules now returns BlockList, a streaming Iterator<Item = i64>. Added Merge (k-way merge over the per-rule Numbers streams) and expand_rules_to_vec for callers that genuinely want the list. core/tests/expand_memory.rs (new, 4 tests, own binary because it installs a global allocator). Two edge-case tests added to core/tests/expand.rs.

WHAT WAS WRONG. expand_rules collected everything into a Vec, then sorted and deduped. At the measured iOS budget of 1.8M entries that is about 14MB held at once inside the Call Directory extension — the process the system picks for its tight memory limit, and the one that tells the app nothing when it is killed. expand_matcher already streamed; this layer undid it.

FIX. Each rule's expansion is already ascending (guaranteed and tested in T010), so the merge needs no buffer. Deduplication is comparing against the last value emitted, which is only sound because the merge is ordered. Numbers are rendered into a reused buffer through a stack array, so a list of millions costs no allocations.

DECISION — a linear scan over the stream heads rather than a BinaryHeap, which the task suggested. k is the number of deny rules, which is small; a scan over k heads is faster at that size and allocates nothing, where a heap allocates and adds log k for no gain. If rule counts ever became large this would be the thing to revisit, but they will not: it is the expansion that is large, not the rule count.

MEASURED, NOT ARGUED. A counting global allocator tracks peak live bytes.
- Streaming a million numbers: peak under one byte per number emitted.
- Collecting the same expansion: at least eight bytes per number, the full list.
- One rule set five times wider than another: peak does not follow the output.
The assertion is stated as a ratio to the output rather than a byte count, because the claim is "not proportional to the list" and a fixed number would have been a guess. Roughly 512KB is live while streaming a million numbers, which is the merge state, two small buffers, and the metadata regex caches warming up.

TWO THINGS THE TEST GOT WRONG FIRST, both worth knowing for anyone writing another one:
1. The counters are global and the harness runs tests in parallel threads, so two overlapping measurements each report the other's allocations. Both initially reported an identical peak, which is what gave it away. All measuring tests now take a mutex.
2. The live counter must be signed. Memory allocated before a measurement began is still freed during it, which underflows an unsigned counter — the first run reported a peak of 18446744073709551608 bytes.

EDGE CASES covered: no deny rules; one; several overlapping; a deny whose pattern rejects everything under it, asserted to leave the result identical to the rule beside it alone; an allow carving a number out of a merged run; streams of very different lengths. The last doubles as an end-to-end dedup proof — the narrow rule's ten numbers sit inside the wide rule's thousand, the union is exactly a thousand, so ten arrived twice and were dropped once each.

VERIFIED. cargo test: 86 pass, 0 fail. Every T010 expansion test passes unchanged. cargo fmt --check clean. cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings clean. tools/check-no-hardcoded-numbering.sh passes. UniFFI bindings still generate.

CORRECTED ALONG THE WAY. An explicit &*DATABASE deref was added to work around what looked like a lifetime error; clippy showed it was unnecessary and the original failure had come from a stale build. Reverted. Also an assertion expecting more than a thousand merged numbers where exactly a thousand is correct.

UNVERIFIED. Nothing has run on a device. The memory figures are host measurements under the system allocator; iOS uses its own, and the extension's actual limit has never been hit deliberately. What is established is the shape — peak does not grow with the list — not an absolute number that will hold on a phone.
